examples.question_text: Find $\int (7e^x-3)\,dx$, including the constant of integration.

examples.solution_text:
The coefficient of $x$ in the exponent is $-4$, so divide by $-4$.
$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}\int 8e^{5-4x}\,dx\\&=\frac{8}{-4}e^{5-4x}+C\\&=-2e^{5-4x}+C\end{aligned}$

Rewrite the reciprocal using a negative exponent.
$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}\int \frac{15}{e^{3x-2}}\,dx\\&=\int 15e^{2-3x}\,dx\\&=\frac{15}{-3}e^{2-3x}+C\\&=-5e^{2-3x}+C\end{aligned}$

Write the cube root as a fractional power of $e$.
$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}\int \sqrt[3]{e^{4x}}\,dx\\&=\int e^{\frac{4x}{3}}\,dx\\&=\frac{1}{\frac{4}{3}}e^{\frac{4x}{3}}+C\\&=\frac{3}{4}e^{\frac{4x}{3}}+C\end{aligned}$

Split the fraction and subtract exponents.
$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}\int \frac{e^{4x}+2e^x}{e^{2x}}\,dx\\&=\int (e^{2x}+2e^{-x})\,dx\\&=\frac{1}{2}e^{2x}-2e^{-x}+C\end{aligned}$

Expand the product, then evaluate the primitive at the upper and lower limits.
$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}\int_0^1 (e^{3x}-2)(e^{3x}+2)\,dx\\&=\int_0^1 (e^{6x}-4)\,dx\\&=\left[\frac{1}{6}e^{6x}-4x\right]_0^1\\&=\left(\frac{e^6}{6}-4\right)-\frac{1}{6}\\&=\frac{e^6-25}{6}\end{aligned}$

examples.question_text: A curve $y=f(x)$ satisfies $f''(x)=9e^{3x}$ and has a stationary point at $(0,4)$. Find $f(x)$.
examples.solution_text:
$\begin{aligned}f'(x)&=\int 9e^{3x}\,dx\\&=3e^{3x}+C_1\end{aligned}$
At the stationary point, $f'(0)=0$.
$\begin{aligned}3+C_1&=0\\C_1&=-3\end{aligned}$
$ f'(x)=3e^{3x}-3$
Integrate again.
$\begin{aligned}f(x)&=\int (3e^{3x}-3)\,dx\\&=e^{3x}-3x+C_2\end{aligned}$
Using $f(0)=4$:
$\begin{aligned}1+C_2&=4\\C_2&=3\end{aligned}$
$ f(x)=e^{3x}-3x+3$

examples.derivation: The exponent derivative is -4, so the primitive is (8/-4)e^(5-4x)+C=-2e^(5-4x)+C. Its derivative is 8e^(5-4x).
Termwise integration gives (3/4)e^(4x)-e^(-2x)+C; differentiation restores both terms.
15/e^(3x-2)=15e^(2-3x). Dividing by -3 gives -5e^(2-3x)+C, whose derivative is the integrand.
The cube root is e^(4x/3); its primitive is (3/4)e^(4x/3)+C.
Splitting gives e^(2x)+2e^(-x). The primitive is (1/2)e^(2x)-2e^(-x)+C.
A primitive is -3e^(5-2x). Upper minus lower gives -3e+3e^3=3(e^3-e).
The product is e^(6x)-4. Evaluating e^(6x)/6-4x from 0 to 1 gives e^6/6-4-1/6=(e^6-25)/6.
Integration gives f(x)=e^(3x-2)+C. At x=2/3, 1+C=4, so C=3. The result satisfies the derivative and given value.
First integration gives f'(x)=3e^(3x)+C1. Stationarity gives C1=-3. Second integration gives f(x)=e^(3x)-3x+C2; f(0)=4 gives C2=3. Both conditions and the second derivative are satisfied.
